question.prompt: Call a fraction \(\dfrac{a}{b},\) not necessarily in the simplest form, special if \(a\) and \(b\) are positive integers whose sum is \(15.\) How many distinct integers can be written as the sum of two, not necessarily different, special fractions?

solutions.title: Group by reduced denominator
solutions.explanation:
Fractions whose sum is an integer must have equal denominators after reduction to lowest terms. Grouping the special fractions this way greatly reduces the number of pairs to examine.

To prove this observation, let \(u/v\) be in lowest terms, and suppose its partner makes the integer \(T\). The partner must equal
\[
T-\frac uv=\frac{Tv-u}{v}.
\]
A common divisor of \(Tv-u\) and \(v\) would also divide \(u\). Since \(u\) and \(v\) have no common divisor greater than \(1\), this expression is already reduced. Thus the partner also has reduced denominator \(v\).

Every special fraction has the form \((15-b)/b\), with \(b=1,2,\ldots,14\). Reducing these fourteen fractions gives the following groups. For each group, examine each fraction paired with itself and with each later fraction, keeping only integer sums.

| Reduced denominator | Special fractions in lowest terms | Distinct integer sums |
|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(2,4,14\) | \(4,6,8,16,18,28\) |
| \(2\) | \(\frac12,\frac32,\frac{13}{2}\) | \(1,2,3,7,8,13\) |
| \(4\) | \(\frac14,\frac{11}{4}\) | \(3\) |
| \(3,7,8,11,13,14\), respectively | \(\frac23,\frac87,\frac78,\frac4{11},\frac2{13},\frac1{14}\) | None |

The last row represents six separate groups, each with just one fraction. None of their doubles is an integer. In the denominator-\(4\) group, the two doubles are not integers, and the only successful pair is
\[
\frac14+\frac{11}{4}=3.
\]
That total already occurs in the denominator-\(2\) group. The first two rows each give six distinct totals, and their only common total is \(8\). Consequently the number of distinct integers is
\[
6+6-1=\boxed{11}.
\]
They are \(1,2,3,4,6,7,8,13,16,18,28\), so the answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutions.title: Search by denominators
solutions.explanation:
Using each denominator to determine its numerator turns the problem into a finite search whose bounds we can justify.

Let the denominators be \(x\) and \(y\). We may assume \(1\le x\le y\le14\), since reversing the two fractions does not change their sum. Equality is allowed. The sum is
\[
\frac{15-x}{x}+\frac{15-y}{y}
=\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{y}-2.
\]
Set
\[
t=\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{y}.
\]
We need integer values of \(t\), and each gives the desired integer sum \(t-2\).

Since both denominators are at most \(14\), we have \(t\ge30/14>2\). If \(x\ge11\), then \(y\ge x\) gives \(t\le30/11<3\), leaving no integer possibility. Thus only \(x=1,2,\ldots,10\) need consideration.

For each fixed \(x\), the bounds \(x\le y\le14\) imply
\[
\frac{15}{x}+\frac{15}{14}\le t\le\frac{30}{x}.
\]
For each integer \(t\) in this interval, solving for \(y\) gives
\[
y=\frac{15x}{tx-15}.
\]
Retain only integer values satisfying \(x\le y\le14\). The successful denominators and their sums are listed in matching order below.

| \(x\) | Candidate integer \(t\) | Successful \(y\) | Sums \(t-2\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(1\) | \(17,18,\ldots,30\) | \(1,3,5\) | \(28,18,16\) |
| \(2\) | \(9,10,\ldots,15\) | \(2,6,10\) | \(13,8,7\) |
| \(3\) | \(7,8,9,10\) | \(3,5\) | \(8,6\) |
| \(4\) | \(5,6,7\) | \(12\) | \(3\) |
| \(5\) | \(5,6\) | \(5\) | \(4\) |
| \(6\) | \(4,5\) | \(6,10\) | \(3,2\) |
| \(7\) | \(4\) | None | None |
| \(8\) | \(3\) | None | None |
| \(9\) | \(3\) | None | None |
| \(10\) | \(3\) | \(10\) | \(1\) |

For example, when \(x=4\), the candidates \(t=5,6,7\) give \(y=12,20/3,60/13\), respectively. Only \(y=12\) works, producing the sum \(3\).

The ordering and bounds cover every allowed pair. Removing repeated totals from the final column leaves
\[
\{1,2,3,4,6,7,8,13,16,18,28\}.
\]
There are \(\boxed{11}\) distinct integers, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
